learning_objectives: Form and recognize regular plural nouns ending in -i or -e.

skills.description_en: Recognise and form -i plurals of regular nouns ending in -o.
Recognise and form -e plurals of regular feminine nouns ending in -a.
Form -i plurals of regular masculine and feminine nouns ending in -e.
Select, correct and produce regular plural nouns in short, meaningful A1 sentences.

lesson.short_explanation_en: Italian generally forms regular noun plurals by changing the final vowel rather than adding -s: -o becomes -i, feminine -a becomes -e, and -e becomes -i for both genders. This lesson uses familiar nouns after numbers such as due and tre; plural articles come in the next lesson.

rule_blocks.heading_en: Regular nouns ending in -o: change to -i
rule_blocks.explanation_en: For the common regular pattern, a singular noun ending in -o changes its final -o to -i in the plural. The noun keeps its gender.
usage_notes_en: The plural noun describes two or more books, plates, people, etc.
Italian normally changes the ending instead of simply adding an English -s.
This lesson covers regular nouns only; not every -o noun behaves this way.
common_errors_en: Wrong: due libro. Correct: due libri.
Wrong: tre libros. Correct: tre libri.

rule_blocks.heading_en: Regular feminine nouns ending in -a: change to -e
rule_blocks.explanation_en: A regular feminine singular noun ending in -a changes its final -a to -e in the plural.
usage_notes_en: Remember the noun’s gender from the previous lesson: not every noun in -a is feminine.
Use a number such as due or tre to make the plural meaning clear.
common_errors_en: Wrong: due penni. Correct: due penne.
Wrong: tre torta. Correct: tre torte.

rule_blocks.explanation_en: Many regular nouns ending in -e have the plural ending -i. This applies to both masculine and feminine nouns.
usage_notes_en: Gender still matters, but both genders use the same -e to -i plural pattern.
This is noun plural formation, not a lesson on plural definite articles.
common_errors_en: Wrong: due fiore. Correct: due fiori.
Wrong: tre chiave. Correct: tre chiavi.

contexts.setting_en: Anna asks Marco, who works in a stationery shop, for several school supplies.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.target: Buongiorno! Vorrei due quaderni e tre penne, per favore.
lines.translation_en: Good morning! I would like two notebooks and three pens, please.

lines.speaker: Marco
lines.translation_en: Certainly. Would you also like two pencils?

lines.speaker: Marco
lines.target: Ecco: due quaderni, tre penne, due matite e tre libri.
lines.translation_en: Here you are: two notebooks, three pens, two pencils and three books.

focus_items.explanation_en: Quaderno ends in -o and changes to -i with a plural number.
Feminine penna ends in -a; the plural ends in -e.
Matita becomes matite, using the regular feminine pattern.
Libri is the regular plural of libro.

contexts.setting_en: Two people get the kitchen ready and bring food for a small gathering.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.target: In cucina Anna mette due piatti e due bicchieri.
lines.translation_en: In the kitchen, Anna puts out two plates and two glasses.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.target: Marco porta tre mele e quattro panini.
lines.translation_en: Marco brings three apples and four bread rolls.

focus_items.explanation_en: The regular plural of piatto is piatti.

examples.note_en: Libri replaces the singular ending -o with -i.
Penna is feminine: the regular plural ends in -e.
The masculine noun fiore takes -i in the plural.

examples.translation_en: I am looking for three keys.
examples.note_en: The feminine noun chiave takes -i in the plural too.

examples.translation_en: I put four plates in the kitchen.
examples.note_en: Piatto follows the regular -o to -i pattern.
Torta is feminine: torta becomes torte.

examples.translation_en: I am waiting for three students.
examples.note_en: Studente is masculine and takes -i in the plural.

examples.translation_en: I can see three cats in the garden.
